peptide.name: PEG-MGF
peptide.summary: PEG-MGF is a pegylated (polyethylene-glycol-conjugated) version of Mechano Growth Factor (MGF), the C-terminal E-domain peptide of the IGF-1Ec splice variant that is naturally expressed within hours of mechanical muscle damage to activate satellite cells. Pegylation extends native MGF's half-life from minutes to hours-to-days. It has essentially no human clinical data and is not FDA-approved; the parent hormone IGF-1 (mecasermin) is separately FDA-approved for a specific pediatric deficiency indication, which should not be conflated with PEG-MGF itself.
peptide.description: MGF (Mechano Growth Factor) is the unique 24-amino-acid C-terminal E-domain peptide produced by alternative splicing of the IGF1 gene, first characterized by Geoffrey Goldspink's laboratory at University College London. Unlike the mature IGF-1 domain (which signals through IGF-1R and is associated with cell proliferation broadly, including in oncology contexts), the MGF E-domain has distinct, more localized biological activity: it is the first IGF-1 splice variant expressed after mechanical muscle damage (within 0-2 hours), peaking at 2-6 hours to activate quiescent satellite cells, before IGF-1Ea expression rises at 6-72 hours to drive differentiation and protein synthesis. Native MGF has an extremely short half-life of approximately 5-7 minutes, severely limiting its practical research utility; PEGylation -- attaching a polyethylene glycol polymer chain -- extends this to hours or days by shielding the peptide from proteolytic degradation and reducing renal clearance, at the cost of introducing a class-wide PEGylation risk: repeated dosing can induce anti-PEG antibodies leading to accelerated clearance on subsequent doses (the 'ABC phenomenon'). PEG-MGF remains entirely preclinical, with animal and cell-culture data on satellite cell activation, and separately-published research on neurogenesis and neuroprotection in brain injury/aging models via the same E-domain peptide. It has no human clinical trial data and is not FDA-approved for any indication.
peptide.mechanism_of_action: Activates quiescent muscle satellite cells (the resident stem-cell population responsible for muscle repair and hypertrophy), expanding the progenitor pool as the first-responding IGF-1 splice variant after mechanical damage. This is mechanistically distinct from mature IGF-1 signaling through IGF-1R (implicated more broadly in cell proliferation, including tumor growth pathways) and from myostatin-inhibition approaches (e.g., follistatin), which remove an anti-growth brake rather than actively recruiting progenitor cells. Separately studied for neurogenic and neuroprotective activity via the same E-domain peptide in brain injury/aging models.
peptide.sequence: IGF-1Ec E-domain C-terminal 24-aa peptide, PEGylated (core peptide MW; total MW varies with PEG chain size)

half_life.note: Native (non-pegylated) MGF has a half-life of only about 5-7 minutes. PEGylation is reported to extend this to hours or even days depending on the specific PEG formulation, but no standardized human pharmacokinetic value has been established.

peptide.evidence_note: PEG-MGF remains entirely preclinical. Supporting data come from rodent and cell-culture studies of satellite cell activation, muscle regeneration, and (separately) neurogenesis/neuroprotection. The related, distinct molecule recombinant IGF-1 (mecasermin) is FDA-approved for severe IGF-1 deficiency, but this approval applies to mature IGF-1, not to PEG-MGF, and should not be read as validation of PEG-MGF itself.
peptide.fda_status_note: Not FDA-approved for any indication and has no human clinical data. Sold as a research chemical 'for research use only.' Do not confuse with FDA-approved recombinant IGF-1 (mecasermin), a distinct molecule.
peptide.compounding_note: Not an FDA-approved drug, no USP monograph, not on the 503A bulks list; not eligible for legal pharmacy compounding.

benefits.label: Satellite cell activation / muscle regeneration (preclinical)
benefits.detail: Activates quiescent satellite cells and expands the muscle progenitor pool in animal and cell-culture models following mechanical damage.

benefits.label: Neurogenesis (preclinical)
benefits.detail: The same MGF E-domain peptide promoted neurogenesis in the aging mouse brain and showed neuroprotective effects in a brain ischemia model in separate published studies.

risks.label: Anti-PEG antibody formation (ABC phenomenon)
risks.detail: Repeated dosing of PEGylated compounds can induce anti-PEG antibodies, potentially causing accelerated clearance and reduced effect on subsequent doses -- a documented class effect of PEGylated therapeutics.

risks.label: IGF-1 pathway / cancer risk (theoretical)
risks.detail: The broader IGF-1R signaling pathway is implicated in cell proliferation and potentially tumor growth in oncology research; the MGF E-domain's relationship to this risk is distinct from mature IGF-1 but not fully characterized.

risks.label: No human safety data
risks.detail: Entirely preclinical; no human trials of any kind have been conducted.

contraindications.label: Personal or family history of IGF-1-pathway malignancy
contraindications.detail: Theoretical concern given the broader IGF-1 signaling pathway's role in some cancers; discuss with a physician.

reconstitution.note: Lyophilized powder reconstituted with bacteriostatic water; concentration depends on diluent volume. Often marketed for localized (intramuscular, near the trained muscle) injection given its short intended radius of action.

lyophilized.stability: Stable when kept cold and dry.

reconstituted.stability: Refrigerate; use within a limited window.

peptide.disclaimer: For research and educational purposes only. This is not medical advice. PEG-MGF is not FDA-approved and has no human clinical trial data. Consult a licensed healthcare provider before using any peptide.

dose_ranges.context: Commonly cited non-clinical use range — NOT validated
dose_ranges.note: Frequently reported anecdotal range, often injected near the specific trained muscle group given its short intended radius of local action. No human trial supports this. Documented for reference only; not a recommendation.

protocols.name: Post-training localized use (anecdotal pattern)
protocols.description: Non-clinical sources describe intramuscular injection near a recently trained muscle group shortly after exercise, based on the rationale that native MGF is naturally expressed within hours of mechanical muscle damage. Summarized only to document the reported pattern.
protocols.cycling_notes: No validated cycling protocol exists in humans.
protocols.disclaimer: Informational summary of anecdotal usage. Not medical advice or a dosing recommendation.
